# Power station size for a refrigerator

**Short answer:** for a typical full-size fridge, get a pure sine wave station with a **surge rating of at least 1,300-1,500 W** and **about 1,000 Wh for roughly half a day, or 1,400-2,000 Wh for a full 24 hours**.

## The three numbers

1. **Running watts:** A full-size fridge draws about 100-250 W while the compressor runs, so almost any 1,000 W-class station covers this ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
2. **Surge watts:** This is the spec that most often fails. Startup spikes are estimated at about 1,000-1,200 W on a typical fridge ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)) and up to 2,400 W on larger or older units ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). Aim for 1,300 W or more ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). Sources disagree on the exact figure, so check your fridge's manual if you can.
3. **Watt-hours:** The compressor only runs about a third of the time. An efficient 18 cu ft fridge averages about 41 W, or roughly 1,400 Wh per day after inverter losses and 20% headroom ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). A large side-by-side with an ice maker can average twice that.

## Quick rules of thumb
- **~1,000 Wh:** about 12-17 hours ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))
- **~1,400-2,000 Wh:** about a full day
- **~2,800 Wh or more:** two days

To size it for your own fridge, take the kWh/year from its yellow EnergyGuide label, multiply by 1,000, and divide by 8,760 to get average watts. Then multiply by hours, divide by 0.85 for inverter losses, and add about 20% headroom. Keep the door closed during the outage. Also, a fridge is unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F with the door shut, so the station needs to be plugged in early.

## Picks that fit
Prices and codes below come from Dealectric's cart tests on Oct 21-25, 2026. These are affiliate-tracked links to the brands' official stores, and the store's checkout has the final word on price.

- **About half a day to a day: [BLUETTI AC180](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac180)**
  - 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W continuous, 2,700 W peak, LiFePO4.
  - $499, or $474.05 with code AFF5OFF.
  - Good for a smaller or efficient fridge.
- **About one day: [ALLPOWERS S2000 Pro](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-s2000-pro-1451wh)**
  - 1,451 Wh, 2,400 W continuous, 4,000 W surge.
  - $664, or $597.60 with code ALLPOWERS26.
  - Roughly matches the 1,400 Wh one-day target.
- **1.5-2 days: [BLUETTI Elite 200 V2](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2)**
  - 2,073 Wh, about 33 hours of fridge runtime by HomeGridHQ's estimate.
  - $899, or $854.05 with code AFF5OFF.
- **Alternative, ~2 kWh: [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)**
  - 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W continuous, 3,000 W peak.
  - $699.99 after coupon.

If you want to back up more than the fridge, such as a freezer, router, or medical device, add their watts and Wh to the totals above.
